turns.doctor_question: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: I’m here because I can’t stop noticing this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. In pictures and in the mirror, one side looks old and beat-up to me. Other people tell me they hardly see anything, but I see it all the time.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports persistent noticing of a perceived rough, sunken facial patch that others reportedly barely notice.

turns.doctor_question: When people tell you they don't notice anything unusual about your skin, is there any part of you that considers they might be right, or are you completely certain that the flaw is really there exactly as you see it?
turns.patient_response: I mean, I hear them, but it’s hard for me to believe it. When I look in the mirror or see a photo, that patch looks rough and sunken to me—like that side of my face looks old and beat-up. I can’t seem to stop seeing it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent perception and preoccupation with a rough, sunken facial patch despite others reporting they barely notice it.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from your concerns about this patch on your face, have you noticed any other unusual beliefs or experiences lately—like feeling that people are watching or talking about you, or hearing or sensing things that others don't?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven’t noticed anything like that. It’s really just the concern about my face.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies unusual beliefs such as feeling watched or talked about.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing or sensing things that others do not.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself doing things like checking the patch in mirrors repeatedly, trying to cover or camouflage it with makeup or your hand, picking at the skin there, or asking others for reassurance about how it looks?
turns.patient_response: Yeah. Before work, or if I’m going to my sister’s game night, I can stand in the bathroom checking it over and over, turning my face under different lights. I rub at the spot too. Sometimes I pull a hat down low, or I just make up an excuse not to go if it looks too obvious to me.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient reports repeatedly checking the spot in mirrors under different lights, rubbing at it, camouflaging it with a hat, and avoiding social activities when it seems too obvious.

turns.doctor_question: If I showed you a photo of your face alongside photos of several other people, and asked you to point out which face had the flaw you're describing, how confident are you that you could convince a neutral stranger who has no stake in the matter that the patch is really there the way you see it?
turns.patient_response: I’d be pretty confident. I mean, in a photo I can see that rough, sunken area right away—it makes that side of my face look older, beat-up. Other people say they barely notice it, but I don’t see how they couldn’t if they really looked.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports high confidence that a rough, sunken facial area is visibly present and remains convinced despite others saying they barely notice it, supporting preoccupation with a perceived appearance flaw.

turns.doctor_question: If you really try, is there any small percentage chance, even just 1%, that this patch might look far less noticeable than you believe, or that your perception could be off?
turns.patient_response: I guess there’s always some tiny chance, but it doesn’t feel that way to me. I see it in the mirror and in photos—that rough, sunken patch—and it makes that side of my face look old and beat-up. People say they barely notice it, but I honestly don’t understand how.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient remains preoccupied with a perceived rough, sunken facial patch seen in mirrors and photos and has difficulty accepting others' reassurance that it is barely noticeable.
